s.d: to process information by giving consideration to various aspects{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages the concept of thinking is closely related to terms referring to perception. For example, in some languages one may speak of thinking as ‘to see with the heart’ or ‘to look at with the liver.’

s.c: In ⟦Matthew 2:16|Matthew 2:16⟧ ἐμπαίζω would seem to carry two closely related meanings, namely ‘to deceive’ and also ‘to make a fool of,’ and therefore it may be quite appropriate to translate this portion of ⟦Matthew 2:16|Matthew 2:16⟧ as ‘when Herod realized that the wise men had deceived him and made a fool of him.’

s.d: to make fun of someone by pretending that he is not what he is or by imitating him in a distorted manner

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: (two different forms of the same base, compare {D:23.18}) to cause someone to be satisfied as the result of food which has been provided in sufficient quantity
s.g: to satisfy with food; to fill with food
s.c: It is possible that in ⟦Luke 1:53|Luke 1:53⟧ the reference is to God’s providence in general rather than merely to feeding the hungry.|A strictly literal rendering of ἐμπίμπλημι or ἐμπιπλάω in the sense of ‘to fill with food’ might carry the wrong implication, namely, ‘to stuff with food’ to the point of making someone extremely uncomfortable. It may therefore be important to divide somewhat the complex semantic components of meaning and to translate ‘to cause to eat much and to become happy’ or ‘to cause to eat enough and as a result to be content.’

s.d: to cause the process of burning to begin
s.g: to ignite; to kindle; to set ablaze; to start a fire; to light a lamp
s.c: As already noted in the series of terms listed in LN 14.63, languages differ appreciably in terms employed for different phases and results of burning. For example, to set something on fire for the sake of providing warmth may be expressed by quite a different term from that which is used in speaking of the process of setting something on fire in order to destroy it.|ἐμπίπρημι refers specifically to the process of setting something on fire, but obviously the implication in ⟦Matthew 22:7|Matthew 22:7⟧ is that the city was burned down. A number of translations, therefore, follow the implied component of ἐμπίπρημι and translate ‘he burned down their city.’ In some languages it may seem strange to speak of ‘burning down a city.’ A more natural expression would be ‘to burn down all the buildings of the city.’

It may therefore be necessary in the case of ⟦Matthew 26:67|Matthew 26:67⟧ to translate ‘they spat in his face’ as ‘they spat in his face to dishonor him’ or ‘… to show their anger against him.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Breathe, Breath
s.d: to breathe upon something
s.c: The process of breathing on someone may have very important symbolic implications. In some instances this can be related to a blessing, as in ⟦John 20:22|John 20:22⟧, but in some languages the act of breathing on a person almost inevitably suggests some harmful influence, often connected with the use of black magic. It may therefore be important to select some less specific term so as to avoid a symbolic meaning which would considerably distort the significance of this one passage in which ἐμφυσάω occurs in the NT.

s.d: a position defined as being within certain limits{N:001}

It may, therefore, be necessary to render this expression in ⟦1 Corinthians 5:9|1 Corinthians 5:9⟧ as ‘part of what I wrote to you about was …’

An equivalent may be ‘in the human heart’ or ‘in people’s hearts.’ In some languages, however, it may be necessary to substitute ‘mind,’ for example, ‘in people’s minds.’

s.g: to be resentful against; to have a grudge against

s.d: to maintain a state of antagonism or hostility
s.g: to be against; to be hostile toward
s.c: In a number of languages hostility is expressed largely in psychological terms, for example, ‘to be angry at’ or ‘to have one’s heart curdle against,’ but hostility may also be expressed in terms of overt behavior, for example, ‘to turn against,’ ‘to face away from,’ or ‘to turn one’s back on.’

s.d: to be under the control of or to be subject to someone or something
s.g: to be subject to; to be under the control of
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult or impossible to maintain the figure of ‘yoke’ in ⟦Galatians 5:1|Galatians 5:1⟧. An equivalent expression may be ‘do not become slaves again’ or ‘do not let people make you slaves again.’ Such a bold metaphor, however, must sometimes be changed to a simile: ‘do not, as it were, let yourselves be made slaves.’

s.d: a position relatively near the speaker, writer, or viewpoint person
s.c: Though ὧδε and ἐνθάδε may seem to be rendered in some contexts as ‘to here’ or ‘hither,’ the semantic component of movement is not found in ὧδε or ἐνθάδε, but in other words in the context indicating movement.

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: extension from a source, with the point of reference near the speaker

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: extension from a source, with the point of reference near the speaker

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Demonstrative or Deictic Reference
s.d: a reference to reason or source
the content of thinking and reasoning
s.c: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to find noun-like words for thinking or reasoning and therefore it may be necessary to use a verb equivalent throughout. For example, in ⟦Luke 11:17|Luke 11:17⟧ one may translate as ‘but Jesus knew what they were thinking.’

s.d: to exist, with respect to particular circumstances

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: the period of a complete year (similar in meaning to {L:ἔτος<SDBG:ἔτος:000000>} ‘year,’ {D:67.167}, but with the focus upon duration)

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: a unit of time of indefinite length, possibly somewhat shorter than {L:αἰών<SDBG:αἰών:000000>}[a] ‘age’ ({D:67.143}) but of a relatively uncertain reference
to happen, with the implication of there being a particular set of circumstances

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: to be simultaneous with the time of the discourse

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: to occur with high probability at a point of time just subsequent to another point of time
to cause someone to regain strength after a temporary loss
s.g: to strengthen again; to cause strength to return

s.d: to regain one’s physical strength after a temporary loss of it
s.c: It may, however, be impossible to say in some languages ‘his strength came back,’ because this would seem to imply a kind of personification of ‘strength.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to translate this phrase in ⟦Acts 9:19|Acts 9:19⟧ as ‘after he had eaten, he became strong again’ or ‘… he was no longer weak.’

s.d: cardinal number, where there are nine instances of a countable entity
s.c: In ⟦Luke 17:17|Luke 17:17⟧ there is a significant ellipsis, and so in some languages one may wish to translate ‘where are the other nine persons?’ or ‘… nine men?’

s.d: to signal to someone by means of part of the body, especially by means of the head or hands{N:001}
s.g: to gesture; to motion; to nod; to beckon
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to be quite specific with regard to types of gestures or motions of the head or hands and arms. For example, in ⟦John 13:24|John 13:24⟧ there is an obvious question involved, and this may require in some languages a particular signal by means of the hands or face. The same would be true in the case of ⟦Luke 1:62|Luke 1:62⟧. In ⟦Luke 1:22|Luke 1:22⟧ the gesture would have to be something which would explain or indicate Zechariah’s inability to speak, while in ⟦Luke 5:7|Luke 5:7⟧ quite another gesture would no doubt be called for, since the persons involved were at quite a distance from one another.

s.d: a particular manner or way of thinking
s.g: way of thinking; disposition; manner of thought; attitude
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to render ‘way of thinking’ by a clause, for example, ‘how people think.’ In the case of ⟦1 Peter 4:1|1 Peter 4:1⟧, it may be necessary to translate ‘you too must strengthen yourselves by thinking just like Christ thought.’

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: that which is intended or purposed as the result of thinking
(derivative of {L:νόμος<SDBG:νόμος:000000>}[a] ‘law, rule,’ {D:33.333}) pertaining to being in accordance with law
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘legal meeting’ would be ‘regular meeting’ or ‘a meeting called by an official’ or ‘a meeting authorized by an official.’

s.d: pertaining to being under obligation imposed by law
s.c: In some languages there is a difficulty involved in rendering ἔννομος by a phrase such as ‘under law,’ since this may be understood in a sense of ‘beneath the law’ or ‘illegal.’ A more common expression would be ‘tied to the law’ or ‘obligated by the law.’

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: pertaining to the period between sunset and sunrise
s.c: In some languages it may be necessary to translate ἔννυχα λίαν in ⟦Mark 1:35|Mark 1:35⟧ as ‘before sunrise’ or ‘long before daylight’ or ‘before the heavens open.’

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐνοικέω ‘to live in,’ not occurring in the NT) to remain in a place defined psychologically or spiritually
s.g: to be in; to live in; to dwell in; to reside in

s.d: a state of oneness
s.c: In some languages it may be strange to speak of ‘that oneness in our faith.’ The closest equivalent may be ‘we believe just as though we were all one person’ or ‘we believe in one and the same way.’

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Cause Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to cause hardship by continual annoyance

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Experience Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to undergo hardship from continual annoyance

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: pertaining to being guilty for having done wrong (primarily a legal term)
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘being guilty’ is expressed in terms of the justification for an accusation. Accordingly, this expression in ⟦1 Corinthians 11:27|1 Corinthians 11:27⟧ may be rendered as ‘he can rightly be accused of sinning against the Lord’s body and blood.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sin, Wrongdoing, Guilt
s.d: pertaining to being guilty and thus deserving some particular penalty
s.g: guilty and deserving; guilty and punishable by

s.d: pertaining to being subject to the control of someone or of some institution
s.g: controlled by; under the control of; subject to
s.c: In this context one may render ἔνοχοι ἦσαν δουλείας as ‘slaves’ and then render the whole expression as ‘as many as were slaves all their lives because of their fear of death’ or ‘… because they were afraid to die.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἐντέλλομαι<SDBG:ἐντέλλομαι:000000>} ‘to command,’ {D:33.329}) that which is authoritatively commanded
to prepare a body for burial{N:001}
s.g: to prepare for burial; preparation for burial

s.d: preparation of a body for burial{N:001}
to give definite orders, implying authority or official sanction
to speak to someone on behalf of someone else
pertaining to being of considerable value or worth

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: pertaining to high status, involving both honor and respect
(derivative of {L:ἐντέλλομαι<SDBG:ἐντέλλομαι:000000>} ‘to command,’ {D:33.329}) that which is authoritatively commanded

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: the inhabitants of a particular place
s.c: A typical rendering of ‘the local people’ is simply ‘the people who lived there’ or ‘those who inhabited that place.’

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Among, Between, In, Inside
s.d: a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects{N:001}
s.c: For another interpretation of ἐντός in ⟦Luke 17:21|Luke 17:21⟧, see discussion at LN 26.1.

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Among, Between, In, Inside
s.d: pertaining to being within an area
s.g: the contents of; that which is inside
s.c: It is also possible, though not probable, to understand ἐντός in ⟦Matthew 23:26|Matthew 23:26⟧ as the inside surface itself rather than the contents.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Shame, Disgrace, Humiliation
s.d: to cause someone to be embarrassed or ashamed

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: to show respect to a person on the basis of his high status
s.c: In a number of languages the showing of respect is referred to by a number of figurative expressions, for example, ‘to bow before,’ ‘to kneel before,’ ‘to crouch before,’ or ‘to stand appalled in the presence of.’

s.d: to provide instruction and training, with the implication of skill in some area of practical knowledge
shaking or trembling, often with the implication of fear and/or consternation
s.c: In a number of languages there are two distinct terms for trembling, one relating to illness (as in the case of epileptic seizures or the chills and fever associated with malaria) and the other associated with fear.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: pertaining to extreme terror or fear, often accompanied by trembling
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 12:21|Hebrews 12:21⟧ the meanings of ἔκφοβος (LN 25.256) and ἔντρομος serve to reinforce each other.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Shame, Disgrace, Humiliation
s.d: a state of embarrassment resulting from what one has done or failed to do{N:001}

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Extravagant Living, Intemperate Living
s.d: to live a life of luxury, usually associated with intemperate feasting and drinking
s.g: to revel; to carouse; to live a life of luxury

s.d: to ask for something with urgency and intensity
s.g: to plead; to beg; to appeal to; to petition
s.c: In translating expressions such as ‘to plead’ or ‘to beg’ or ‘to appeal to,’ the implications of urgency or intensity are often expressed in figurative ways, for example, ‘to ask for with the heart exposed’ or ‘to ask for with crying words’ or ‘to beg with one’s hands outstretched.’

s.d: to speak to someone on behalf of someone else
to enclose an object by winding something about or around it
to cause something to be in the shape of a roll{N:001}
s.g: to roll up; to make into a roll

s.d: to cut or incise letters or designs
s.g: to cut; to carve; to engrave

s.d: to speak against someone in an insolent and arrogant way
to experience dreams having the significance of visions
s.c: For a discussion of some of the problems involved in terms for ‘dream,’ see LN 33.486.

s.d: a dream as a means of communication{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘dream’ depending upon the nature of the dream. A frightening dream without special significance or a dream with erotic implications may be referred to by terms which are quite different from a term referring to a dream which carries important meaning, in other words, a dream which constitutes a type of vision or symbol of some reality.

s.dp: Spacial Positions › In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
s.d: a position in front of an object, whether animate or inanimate, which is regarded as having a spacial orientation of front and back{N:001}
(with the genitive) marking a participant whose viewpoint is relevant to an event{N:002}
s.g: in the sight of; in the opinion of; in the judgment of
s.c: It is also possible to interpret ἐνώπιον in ⟦Luke 12:6|Luke 12:6⟧ as a marker of agent (Domain 90A) as in TEV, “not one of them is forgotten by God.”
